entries.name: eq_any_operands_bare-errored#0
entries.script: [G1] `ByIndex(t,0) == ByIndex(t,1)` — BOTH operands `SAny`, so the deserialization builder's SameType check is SATISFIED and the tree PARSES (it even re-writes byte-identically); the throw is at eval, `RuntimeException: Unknown type SAny`, because `isValueOfType` has no `SAny` case. **SEPARATING:** an implementation that compares the two items here over-accepts — and one that refuses the tree at PARSE is also wrong, just invisibly so on this tier (the wire family grades that).

entries.name: eq_any_operands_sigmaprop-errored#1
entries.script: [G2] The same comparison under `sigmaProp` — the REACHABLE form, since this is a tree a box can actually carry (G1's bare Boolean root cannot be a script). Same parse, same throw at eval — `Unknown type SAny` — and the spend it guards therefore fails. **SEPARATING,** and the row that gives the gate consensus teeth.

entries.name: eq_control_coll_items-accept#2
entries.script: [C1] **CONTROL for G1** — the same double-`ByIndex` equality over `Coll[Int](1,2,3)`: **false at cost 83**. Two items, same shapes, and it answers; so G1's throw is the `SAny` item type and not the comparison of two indexed items.

entries.name: eq_control_coll_sigmaprop-accept#3
entries.script: [C2] **CONTROL for G2** — the same under `sigmaProp`: a `SigmaProp` (false) at cost 98.

entries.name: plus_node_left_any-errored#4
entries.script: [G3] `ByIndex(t,0) + 1` — **`KeyNotFoundException: key 97`**. Nothing checks the operand at parse; `ArithOp.eval` looks its implementation up by the LEFT operand's type code, and 97 is `SAny`. The message names no type, which is worth knowing before matching on text. **SEPARATING:** sigma-rust evaluated this to 2 at `eda571a6`.

entries.name: plus_method_left_any-errored#5
entries.script: [G4] The same arithmetic with the item fetched by the `apply` METHOD instead of the `ByIndex` node — `(1,2,3).apply(0) + 1`. Same `key 97`. The pair G3/G4 matters because the two routes to the item differ elsewhere (`map` works as a node and not as a method), and here they do NOT: the gate is the arithmetic, not the fetch. This is the sigma-rust addendum's K1, reachable on its fork master today. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: min_method_left_any-errored#6
entries.script: [G5] `min((1,2,3).apply(0), 1)` — the addendum's K5. `min` is a different `ArithOpCompanion` with its own opcode and it fails identically, `KeyNotFoundException: key 97`, which is what shows the fault is the shared table lookup rather than `Plus`. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: plus_node_right_any-accept#7
entries.script: [G6] `1 + ByIndex(t,0)` — **2 at cost 60. THE ASYMMETRY:** the same two values, the operands swapped, and it ANSWERS, because the implementation is chosen by the LEFT operand's type (`SInt`) and the right one is never consulted for it. **SEPARATING the other way:** an implementation that refuses an `Any`-typed operand wherever it appears OVER-REJECTS a tree the JVM evaluates.

entries.name: plus_method_right_any-accept#8
entries.script: [G7] `1 + (1,2,3).apply(0)` — the addendum's K2, **2 at cost 64**, which is the number it asked for. Identical to C4, its plain-collection control: the `Any`-typed right operand is FREE. **SEPARATING the other way.**

entries.name: min_method_right_any-accept#9
entries.script: [G8] `min(1, (1,2,3).apply(0))` — **1 at cost 54**, identical to C5. The asymmetry holds for `min` too, so an implementation cannot fix G5 by refusing the type in both positions. **SEPARATING the other way.**

entries.name: plus_node_control-accept#10
entries.script: [C3] **CONTROL for G3/G6** — `ByIndex(Coll[Int](1,2,3),0) + 1` is 2 at cost **60**, the same as G6. The arithmetic costs what it costs; the representation adds nothing.

entries.name: plus_method_control-accept#11
entries.script: [C4] **CONTROL for G4/G7** — the `apply`-method form over an ordinary collection: 2 at cost **64**, equal to G7 and 4 dearer than the node form, which is the method call's own cost.

entries.name: min_method_control-accept#12
entries.script: [C5] **CONTROL for G5/G8** — 1 at cost **54**, equal to G8.

entries.name: fold_tuple_accumulator-errored#13
entries.script: [G9] `Fold(Coll[Int](1,2,3), (1,2,3), p => p._1).size` — the tuple as the ACCUMULATOR. The zero is a `Value.checkType` site, and `isValueOfType` throws **"Unsupported tuple type"** for any arity but 2 (`SType.scala:202`) — a different refusal from the `SAny` ones above: it is the tuple VALUE being rejected, not an operand's type. `Tuple.non_pair_value_ops` T11/C11 hold the accepting twin, where the accumulator is an `Int` and the same tuple is the INPUT. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: concrete_collection_of_tuples-errored#14
entries.script: [G10] `SizeOf(Coll((1,2,3), (1,2,3)))` — a `ConcreteCollection` whose ITEMS are non-pair tuples. Every item goes through the same `checkType` site — the same **"Unsupported tuple type"** as G9 — so the collection cannot be built AT ALL and the throw precedes any operation on it. **The other half of this is not authorable yet:** the identical collection arriving in a REGISTER evaluates (`3` at cost 124, measured), so the JVM's answer depends on where the collection came from — the same provenance shape as `Coll.runtime_shapes_methodcall` B1/B3 — but the eval tier's input decoder cannot express a non-pair tuple today, so the register half waits on that. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: concrete_collection_of_pairs_control-accept#15
entries.script: [C6] **CONTROL for G10** — the same shape built from PAIRS: `SizeOf(Coll((1,2), (3,4)))` is **2 at cost 84**. `ConcreteCollection` takes pairs happily, so G10 is about the ARITY and not about building a collection of tuples.
